oneSentence: A citation in an AI answer points you to the source passage or document used to support a specific claim.
plainExplanation:
When an AI system gives an answer with citations, it shows where parts of that answer came from. The source might be a web page, a report, a policy document or a passage from a knowledge base. The useful part is not the label alone, but the link between the claim and the supporting text.

A common process starts with a question. The system searches a set of documents and retrieves passages that seem relevant. “Retrieve” here means find and bring back likely source text. The model then drafts an answer and attaches references to the passages it used.

What goes in is your question and a collection of documents. What happens is search, selection and answer drafting. What comes out is an answer plus citations, often as footnotes, numbered references or quoted snippets.

A citation is not the same as proof. It can point to a weak source, the wrong passage or a passage that only partly supports the answer. It is also not the same as grounding. Grounding is the broader idea of tying an answer to external material; a citation is the visible pointer that helps a person check that connection.

For a reader, the main value is verification. You can open the cited source, see the original wording, check the date and judge whether the answer represented it fairly.

everydayAnalogy.title: Matching a photographed form to the right template
everydayAnalogy.story: A clinic worker in Nairobi receives a phone photo of a paper form. The image is unclear, so she compares it with a folder of known form templates and finds the one with the same layout and field labels. When she tells her colleague which form it is, she also clips the matching template page to her note so the colleague can check it directly. The clipped page does not guarantee that every handwritten entry was read correctly, but it gives everyone a concrete place to verify the match.

mapping.analogyElement: the phone photo of the form

mapping.aiElement: the document collection or knowledge base
the retrieved source passage or document

mapping.analogyElement: clipping the template page to the note
mapping.aiElement: adding a citation to the answer

everydayAnalogy.limitation: In the story, a person deliberately compares visible layouts. In AI systems, matching is often done mathematically from text or embeddings, which are numerical representations of meaning-like patterns. Also, a cited passage in an AI answer may support only one sentence or part of a sentence, not the whole answer. The analogy also makes the match seem clearer than it often is: real retrieval can return several partly relevant passages, and the model may cite one imperfectly.

visual.title: How citations get attached to an AI answer
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, a reader should be able to say that citations come from retrieved source passages and are there to help people verify claims.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow with five boxes connected by arrows. Read from the user’s question to document search, then retrieved passages, then drafted answer, then answer with citation markers linked back to the passages. Small callout text under the final box says: “Helpful for checking, not automatic proof.”

steps.label: Question
steps.explanation: A person asks something, such as a factual or policy question.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a rounded rectangle labelled “Question” with a short sample query inside.

steps.label: Search documents
steps.explanation: The system looks through a document set for passages that appear relevant.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second rounded rectangle labelled “Search documents”. Show stacked document icons behind it.

steps.label: Retrieve passages
steps.explanation: A few passages are selected as possible support for the answer.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a third box labelled “Retrieved passages” with 2 to 3 short text snippets in quotation marks.

steps.label: Draft answer
steps.explanation: The model uses the retrieved text to draft a response.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a fourth box labelled “Draft answer” with 2 short answer lines. Use an arrow from retrieved passages to this box.

steps.label: Show citations
steps.explanation: Citation markers point from answer claims back to the supporting passages so a person can inspect them.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a final box labelled “Answer with citations”. Add superscript numbers after two claims and thin connector lines from those numbers back to matching snippets in the retrieved passages box.

visual.interaction: On hover or tap of a citation marker, highlight the matching source snippet and dim the others.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram shows a five-step process. First, a user asks a question. Second, the system searches a collection of documents. Third, it retrieves a small number of relevant passages. Fourth, the model drafts an answer using those passages. Fifth, the answer displays citation markers, such as small numbers, that point back to the specific passages. The main message is that citations are pointers to supporting text, so a person can verify claims, but the presence of a citation alone does not guarantee the answer is correct.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static five-box flow chart appears from left to right: Question, Search documents, Retrieved passages, Draft answer, and Answer with citations. Thin lines connect citation numbers in the last box back to source snippets in the retrieved passages box.

workedExample.scenario: A staff member asks an internal assistant: “What is the deadline for travel reimbursement claims?”
workedExample.input: Question plus an approved internal travel policy collection.
process: The system searches the policy documents and retrieves two passages: one says claims should be submitted within 30 days of trip completion, and another describes exceptions for medical emergencies.
The model drafts an answer: “Travel reimbursement claims should normally be submitted within 30 days after the trip ends, with limited exceptions for medical emergencies.”
The answer shows citation [1] after “30 days” and citation [2] after “medical emergencies”.
The staff member opens both cited passages and confirms that the wording matches the policy version currently in force.
workedExample.result: The user receives a short answer with two citations that make checking fast and transparent.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A communications officer is reviewing a draft summary of programme monitoring data and asks an approved internal assistant to identify the sections of the latest public report that support each summary sentence.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Citations help the officer check that the summary matches the published source before it is shared, which reduces the risk of misquoting trends or dates.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload personal data, beneficiary records, protection-sensitive information or unpublished confidential monitoring data into an unapproved public AI service; use only approved systems and keep human review.

whyItMatters: For non-specialists, citations change an AI answer from something you can only read into something you can inspect. That matters when a sentence may affect a briefing, a public statement, a procurement note or a policy discussion. A citation helps you ask practical questions: Where did this come from? Is the source authoritative? Is it current? Does the source really support this exact claim? Without that check, an answer can sound confident while resting on weak or mismatched material. With citations, verification becomes faster, but it still depends on human judgement.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If an AI answer has citations, the answer is reliable.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Citations help, but reliability depends on what was cited and how accurately the answer used it. A system can attach an outdated source, cite a passage that only partly supports the claim, or misread the passage. You still need to inspect the source.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A citation always points to the exact sentence that proves the claim.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Some systems cite a whole document, a page or a chunk of text rather than the precise line. That can still be useful, but it means the reader may need to look around the cited passage and judge whether the support is strong enough.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Citation and grounding mean the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are related, but not identical. Grounding is the broader practice of tying an answer to external evidence or data. A citation is the visible reference shown to the user. A system can attempt grounding without showing clear citations, and a citation can be shown even if the support is weak.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A citation is the “show me where that came from” part of an AI answer.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In retrieval-augmented systems, citations are usually produced after a retrieval step selects relevant documents or chunks from an indexed collection. The model then generates a response conditioned on that retrieved context, and the interface attaches references to the source items, passages or spans. Depending on the system design, the citation may be linked before generation, during generation or by a later alignment step. Citation quality depends on retrieval quality, chunking, ranking, source metadata and how accurately the system maps answer claims back to evidence. This is why a citation is best treated as traceability support, not as a guarantee of factual correctness.

keyTakeaway: A good citation lets you trace an AI claim back to source text, but you still need to check whether the source truly supports the claim.

quickCheck.question: What is the main purpose of a citation in an AI answer?
options: To make the answer sound more academic
To point the reader to the source used so the claim can be checked
To guarantee that the answer is correct
To replace the need to read the original document
quickCheck.explanation: The core job of a citation is traceability. It helps a reader inspect the original source and judge whether the answer used it correctly. It does not by itself guarantee accuracy, and it does not remove the need for human review.
